read: partial: main text pp.1-10 and appendix A.1, A.2.7-A.3.5 and A.4 (pp.13, 22-27, 30-32) read; the worked derivations in A.2.1-A.2.6 skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2410.09988v2, 13 Dec 2024, marked 'A PREPRINT' (p.1); the text shows no peer-reviewed venue
what_it_is: HARDMath is a dataset of graduate-level applied mathematics problems inspired by a course on asymptotic methods: nondimensionalisation of polynomials, polynomial roots and root corrections, nonlinear third-order ODEs, and traditional and Laplace integrals, to be solved with approximate analytical methods such as dominant balance (p.1, p.3-6). Problems and step-by-step solutions are generated by code (SymPy, SciPy) from randomly selected coefficients, functional forms and initial conditions, and kept only if the approximate solution is within 10% of a numerical solution (p.4-5). It has 1,466 problems: 1,060 for development, the 366-problem evaluation set HARDMath-mini, and 40 hand-written word problems in applied-science contexts (p.1, p.4, p.10). Answers are checked automatically (boxed answer, SymPy equivalence and numerical evaluation), and for three problem types GPT-4o also grades responses against the answer key with rubrics adapted from course grading guidelines (p.7, p.25); o1-mini with 5-shot CoT scores 62.3% and GPT-4 43.8% (p.7-8).
domain: applied mathematics (asymptotic and approximate analytical methods), plus 40 word problems in applied-science contexts
size: 1,466 problems: 1,060 development, 366 HARDMath-mini evaluation, 40 word problems (p.1, p.4, p.10); five models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, o1-mini, Llama3-8b, CodeLlama-13b (p.7-8)
source_of_items: generated by algorithms (SymPy, SciPy) from random coefficients, functional forms and initial conditions (p.4); the 40 word problems were written by hand (p.4, p.6)
instances: generated (released as fixed sets; the code can generate any number of further problems, p.2, p.10)
has_gold_traces: yes: every problem has a generated step-by-step LaTeX solution embedded in explanatory text, with boxed final answers, validated against numerical solutions (p.4-5)
evaluation: final answer (boxed; SymPy equivalence checks and numerical evaluation) plus LLM judge: GPT-4o grades Roots, ODEs and Integrals responses against the answer key with partial credit (p.7). The rubrics score the regime-by-regime answers; only the Laplace-integral rubric gives credit for reaching an intermediate checkpoint (p.25). This is partial-credit grading, not a step-by-step verification of the response.
human_validation: HARDMath-mini and the word problems are called human-verified (p.10): analytical solutions were plotted against numerical ground truth for visual checking (p.5, p.13), and every problem passed the 10% error filter (p.5); the authors call step-by-step manual verification impractical (p.5). The GPT-4o grader was checked by manually verifying an unspecified subset of its grades, with average adjustments per model and problem type between -0.15 and +0.07 (Table 6, p.26). No agreement statistics are reported.
contamination_measures: none stated; the generator could produce new problems (p.2, p.10), but the paper does not present this as a contamination measure

engtrace_use.sentence: S-M1 (L155-161): In mathematics, benchmarks ranging from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) to HardMath (Fan et al., 2024), Putnam-Axiom (Gulati et al., 2024), and GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al., 2024) rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability.
engtrace_use.explanation: HARDMath does not fit 'abstract logical deduction': it is applied mathematics built on approximation, numerical checks and 'subjective judgment' (p.1, p.4), and its authors set it against datasets that 'focus on abstract, formal mathematics' (p.2). It does not measure 'reasoning stability'. More important for EngTrace, the sentence files it with outcome-scored mathematics benchmarks and omits the features EngTrace presents as its own: HARDMath generates problems together with step-by-step solutions by code, validates the gold answers numerically (p.4-5), and grades beyond the final answer with a rubric-based LLM judge and partial credit (p.7, p.25), in a field motivated by science and engineering problems (p.1-2). Read with S-E3 ('existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching'), the May text misrepresents this paper. The name is HARDMath, not HardMath.

suggested_wording: HARDMath (Fan et al., 2024) generates graduate-level applied-mathematics problems and their step-by-step solutions by code, keeps only answers within 10% of a numerical solution, and adds GPT-4o rubric grading with partial credit to the final-answer check.
facts_to_cite: 1,466 problems: 1,060 for development, 366 in the evaluation set HARDMath-mini, and 40 hand-written word problems (p.1, p.4, p.10)

Problem types: polynomial nondimensionalisation, polynomial roots and root corrections, nonlinear third-order ODEs, traditional and Laplace integrals, solved by asymptotic methods such as dominant balance (p.3-6)
Problems and step-by-step solutions are generated with SymPy and SciPy from random coefficients, functional forms and initial conditions, without duplicates (p.4)
Only problems whose approximate solutions lie within 10% of numerical ground truth are kept (p.5)
HARDMath-mini was verified by plotting analytical against numerical solutions; step-by-step manual verification was judged impractical (p.5, p.13)
Scoring combines a boxed-answer check (SymPy equivalence and numerical evaluation) with GPT-4o grading against rubrics adapted from course grading guidelines for Roots, ODEs and Integrals (p.7)
The rubrics give partial credit by solution regime; the Laplace-integral rubric awards half credit for reaching an intermediate checkpoint (p.25)
A manual check of a subset of GPT-4o grades gave average adjustments between -0.15 and +0.07 per model and problem type (Table 6, p.26)
With 5-shot CoT, o1-mini scores 62.3%, GPT-4 43.8% and Llama3-8b 20.2% (p.7-8); GPT-4 scores 28.1% on the word problems (p.8)
A preliminary pipeline used one LLM to wrap 30 ODE problems in physics contexts and a second LLM to score their plausibility (p.6, p.22-23)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: problems and step-by-step solutions generated by code from randomised parameters (p.4), which is EngTrace's template mechanism in another field; numerical validation of the gold answers (p.5); evaluation beyond a single final-answer match, with partial credit (p.7); a manual check of the LLM grader (p.7, p.26); applied problems of the kind met in science and engineering (p.1). Lacks: engineering domains, units and physical data; deterministic checking of intermediate steps (the GPT-4o rubrics mostly score regime-wise answers, with one checkpoint rule, p.25); expert validation of the grader with agreement statistics (only average adjustments on a subset of unstated size, p.26); contamination framing; a private pool (HARDMath-mini is a fixed public set).
notes: The closest mathematics precedent for EngTrace's combination of a generated problem with a generated gold solution and for grading beyond the final answer; the revised text should credit it rather than imply that the combination is new, and the claim that no benchmark verifies the process (May L77-80) and S-E3 need qualifying in its light. The sizes add up only as 1,060 + 366 + 40 = 1,466 (p.1, p.4, p.10), although the abstract calls HARDMath-mini 'sub-sampled' (p.1). The text shows only arXiv v2; whether a peer-reviewed version exists should be checked before the reference is finalised (I did not consult the web). The May reference entry (L959) matches the nine authors on p.1.
